--- aliases: - 01-setup-and-first-look.html title: "Session 1: R Basics, Importing, and Inspecting Data" subtitle: "Objects, functions, packages, and project folders, then your first dataset" --- ::: downloads [⬇ Student script](https://github.com/CWML/CWML-R-Hands-on-Workshop-Series/blob/main/student_scripts/Session%201%20-%20R%20Basics%2C%20Importing%2C%20and%20Inspecting_STUDENT.R){.btn .btn-outline-primary .btn-sm} [⬇ Solutions](https://github.com/CWML/CWML-R-Hands-on-Workshop-Series/blob/main/solutions/Session%201%20-%20R%20Basics%2C%20Importing%2C%20and%20Inspecting_SOLUTIONS.R){.btn .btn-outline-secondary .btn-sm} [⬇ Workshop folder (ZIP)](https://github.com/CWML/CWML-R-Hands-on-Workshop-Series/releases/download/student-files/cwml-r-workshop.zip){.btn .btn-outline-secondary .btn-sm} ::: ::: callout-note ## In this session you will learn to 1. Create objects and call functions 2. Install packages (once) and load them (every session) 3. Open the workshop's project folder and use `here()` to build file paths that work on any computer 4. Import a data file with `import()` and `here()` 5. Inspect a dataset with `dim()`, `glimpse()`, `skim()`, and `count()` 6. Tell errors, warnings, and messages apart, and fix code that doesn't run 7. Write down a list of the problems that need cleaning **Before you start:** complete the [Setup](../setup.qmd) and open `student_scripts/Session 1 - R Basics, Importing, and Inspecting_STUDENT.R`. ::: **Where this session fits.** Most data projects go through the same steps, whatever the topic. Today covers the first two, **Import** and **Inspect** (highlighted): getting the data into R, and looking at it carefully before changing anything. You could do these steps in Excel or SPSS too. What R adds is that every step is written down in a script, so you (or a colleague) can check it, rerun it on next month's data, and share it. ::: workflow 1. [Import]{.step .today} 2. [Inspect]{.step .today} 3. [Clean]{.step} 4. [Combine]{.step} 5. [Reshape]{.step} 6. [Summarize]{.step} 7. [Visualize]{.step} 8. [Save and share]{.step} 9. [Automate]{.step} ::: # Part 1: R basics Before we open any data, a few building blocks you'll use in every line of R. Type these in your script and run each line with **Cmd + Return** (Mac) or **Ctrl + Enter** (Windows); the result appears in the **Console**. ## Objects and the assignment arrow `<-` `<-` stores a value in an **object** so you can use it later. Read it as "gets". The object appears in the **Variables** pane. Shortcut: **Option + -** (Mac) or **Alt + -** (Windows) types `<-` for you. ::: follow-along **👀 Follow along 1.1** — Store a number in an object called `my_age`, then add 5 to it. Pattern: `OBJECT_NAME <- VALUE` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_age <- 35 my_age ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 35 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} my_age + 5 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 40 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## 🔍 What this code does - `my_age <- 35` creates an object called `my_age` and stores the number 35 in it. Nothing prints: saving is silent. `my_age` now appears in the **Variables** pane. - `my_age` on its own prints what is stored: `[1] 35`. The `[1]` means "this is the first value". It helps you keep your place when the output runs over several lines. - `my_age + 5` uses the object in a calculation and prints 40. `my_age` itself is still 35: to change it, you would save again with `<-`. ::: ## Vectors `c()` combines values into a **vector**. Every value in a vector has the same type. Text values need quotes: `c("Central Hospital", "Other")`. ::: follow-along **👀 Follow along 1.2** — Make a vector of ages with `c()`, then find the `mean()`. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ages <- c(2, 18, 56, 61) mean(ages) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 34.25 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## 🔍 What this code does - `c(2, 18, 56, 61)` combines four numbers into one vector, and `ages <-` saves it. - `mean(ages)` gives the whole vector to `mean()`, which adds the values and divides by how many there are: (2 + 18 + 56 + 61) / 4 = 34.25. - Most R functions work on a whole vector at once, so you rarely handle values one by one. ::: ## Functions and arguments A **function** does something to its inputs (**arguments**): `function_name(argument1, argument2, ...)`. Arguments can be named. ::: follow-along **👀 Follow along 1.3** — Use `round(3.14159)` with and without `digits = 2`. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} round(3.14159) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} round(3.14159, digits = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.14 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## 🔍 What this code does - `round(3.14159)` has one argument, the number. The `digits` argument wasn't given, so `round()` uses its default, 0, and rounds to a whole number: 3. - `round(3.14159, digits = 2)` adds a second, **named** argument and gives 3.14. - Arguments you leave out use their default value. The help page (`?round`) lists every argument and its default. ::: ::: callout-tip ## Getting help Type `?round` in the Console to open the help page for any function. ::: ## Data frames A **data frame** is a table: each **column** is a variable (a vector), each **row** is an observation. (Later you'll also see **tibbles**: the tidyverse version of a data frame, which prints more neatly.) Here is a small data frame called `patients`, drawn as boxes. Each **column** is a vector, so every value in it has the same type: `name` is all text and `age` is all numbers. Each **row** is one patient. ```{=html}
name
"Ana"
"Ben"
"Cho"
text
age
34
51
27
numbers
``` This is the code that makes it. **You don't need to type it**: you'll build data frames yourself in Session 4. Notice `$`, which pulls out one column; you'll use it often. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} patients <- data.frame( name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cho"), age = c(34, 51, 27) ) patients ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` name age 1 Ana 34 2 Ben 51 3 Cho 27 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} patients$age # $ pulls out one column ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 34 51 27 ``` ::: ::: ::: callout-warning ## Common mistakes - R is **case-sensitive**: `Age` and `age` are different - Object names can't start with a number or contain spaces: `age2` and `my_age` work, `2age` and `my age` don't. Avoid names R already uses, such as `c`, `mean`, or `data` - Text needs quotes (`"Central Hospital"`); object names do not (`my_age`) - Every `(` needs a `)` — Positron highlights the matching pair - `#` starts a comment; R ignores the rest of the line ::: ::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false} ## ✏️ TRY IT 1 (2 min): objects and functions Store three temperatures, 38.5, 39.1, and 37.9, in an object called `my_temps`. Then find their `mean()`. ✅ **Check:** the mean is 38.5 ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false} ## Show solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} my_temps <- c(38.5, 39.1, 37.9) mean(my_temps) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 38.5 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## 📖 Good to know - **Script or Console?** The Console runs a line once and forgets it. Your script is the record of what you did, so type your code in the script and run it from there. - **Objects live in R's memory, not on your disk.** They disappear when you close Positron or restart R. That's fine: rerun your script and they're back. If you're ever asked whether to save the workspace, choose **No**. - **`<-` or `=`?** Both can store a value, but this course always uses `<-`, so that `=` only ever means "name an argument" (as in `digits = 2`). - **A vector holds one type.** If you mix text into numbers, R turns everything into text: `c(5, 12, "unknown")` is three pieces of text. You'll see this in the practice data, where a few ages say "unknown". ::: # Part 2: Installing and loading packages A **package** is a collection of functions someone else wrote. There are two steps: | Step | Function | How often | Analogy | |---------|----------------------|---------------------------|-------------------------| | Install | `install.packages()` | **Once** per computer | Buying a book | | Load | `library()` | **Every** time you open R | Taking it off the shelf | To install **one** package, put its name in quotes: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages("janitor") ``` ::: To install **several** at once, combine the names with `c()`, the same `c()` you used for vectors in Part 1. This line installs everything for the whole workshop series (skip it if you did the [Setup](../setup.qmd)): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} install.packages(c("tidyverse", "here", "rio", "janitor", "skimr", "gtsummary", "flextable", "scales")) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## 🔍 What this code does - `install.packages("janitor")` downloads one package, janitor, from CRAN (R's official package library, see below) and installs it on your computer. Some packages need a few others to work: R installs those too, so you may see several downloads. - `install.packages(c(...))` does the same for every name in the list, one after the other. It can take several minutes. - You install a package **once** per computer. You only need to install it again after you install a new version of R, or to get a newer version of the package. ::: Load only what you need today: ::: follow-along **👀 Follow along 2.1** — Load today's packages, one `library()` line each. ✅ You should see no line that starts with "Error". Pattern: `library(PACKAGE_NAME)` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) # data wrangling (dplyr) and plotting (ggplot2) library(here) # file paths that work on any computer library(rio) # import() and export() for almost any file type library(skimr) # skim() for a quick data summary ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## 🔍 What this code does - Each `library()` line makes one package's functions available until you close Positron or restart R. That's why every session starts with these lines. - `library(tidyverse)` loads a whole family of packages at once (dplyr, ggplot2, tidyr, readr, stringr, forcats, lubridate, tibble, and purrr) and lists them. - Its **Conflicts** message says that a few tidyverse functions share a name with a base R function, for example `filter()`. From now on, `filter()` means the tidyverse version. This is normal, not an error. - The text after `#` is a **comment**: a note for people. R ignores it. ::: ::: callout-warning ## Common mistakes - Package names need quotes in `install.packages()` but **not** in `library()`. - Red text is not always an error! See the next section. ::: ## Error, warning, or message? You just saw red text in the Console. Red text comes in three kinds, and each one asks something different of you: | Kind | How to spot it | What happened | What to do | |---|---|---|---| | **Error** | starts with `Error` | R stopped. The line did nothing. | Read the message, fix the code, run it again | | **Warning** | starts with `Warning` | R finished, but something may be off | Check the result: did values turn into `NA`, or did rows disappear? | | **Message** | anything else, like the list from `library(tidyverse)` | Information only | Nothing | The message after `Error` usually tells you what's wrong, for example `could not find function "Count"` (R is case-sensitive: the function is `count()`). You'll practise reading them in TRY IT 5. ::: callout-tip ## Asking for help Stuck? Put up your red sticky note. When you ask someone for help, in class, by email, or online, include three things: 1. **Which line** you ran (copy it) 2. **What you expected** to happen 3. **The exact message** R gave you (copy it, don't retype it) ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## 📖 Good to know - Packages are shared on **CRAN**, R's official package library, which has more than 20,000 of them. `install.packages()` downloads from there. - The **tidyverse** is a family of packages designed to work together, with the same style of function names and arguments. That's why one `library(tidyverse)` loads several of them. ::: # Part 3: Project folders and `here()` ## Why keep everything in one project folder? - **Organization:** data, scripts, and outputs live in one folder with a predictable structure (`raw_data/`, `processed_data/`, `student_scripts/`) - **Reproducibility:** the project works on any computer — yours, a collaborator's, future you's - **Shareable:** zip the folder and send it, or put it on GitHub ## Open the project folder for this class 1. Download the workshop folder and save it somewhere you can find it (not your Downloads folder) 2. In Positron, choose **File → Open Folder...**, select the `cwml-r-workshop` folder, and click **Open**. Positron uses that folder as the working directory 3. Check the **Explorer** on the left: it should list the workshop files (`raw_data`, `student_scripts`, ...) ::: callout-tip ## Your own projects later Make a new folder for each project (with subfolders like `raw_data/` and `scripts/`), and open it in Positron with **File → Open Folder...**. Add an empty file called `.here` at the top so `here()` always finds it. ::: ## Relative vs absolute paths - **Bad (absolute):** `"/Users/mwegener/Desktop/maybe_here/data.csv"` — only works on one computer - **Good (relative):** `here("raw_data", "data.csv")` — works on any computer that has the project folder `here()` finds the top of the project folder (it looks for a `.here` file, which the workshop folder has) and builds the path from there. ::: follow-along **👀 Follow along 3.1** — Find the top of the project folder. Pattern: `here::here()` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} here::here() # where is the top of my project? ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## 🔍 What this code does - `here::here()` prints the full path to the top of the project folder: wherever you saved `cwml-r-workshop` on your computer. It finds the top by looking for the `.here` file. - If the path isn't your workshop folder, the folder isn't open in Positron. Choose **File → Open Folder...** and open it. ::: ::: follow-along **👀 Follow along 3.2** — Build the path to `raw_data/linelist_raw.xlsx`. Pattern: `here::here("FOLDER", "FILE_NAME.EXTENSION")` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} here::here("raw_data", "linelist_raw.xlsx") # full path to a file inside it ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## 🔍 What this code does - `here::here("raw_data", "linelist_raw.xlsx")` adds a folder and a file name to that path, joined with `/`. R uses `/` on every computer, Windows included. - It only **builds** the path, as text. It doesn't check that the file exists or open it: that's the job of `import()`, next. - Each piece is in quotes because it's text, not the name of an object. ::: `here::here()` means "the `here()` function from the here package". The `::` lets you use a function before loading its package. ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## 📖 Good to know - The **working directory** is the folder R reads files from and saves files to. Opening the workshop folder in Positron sets it for you. - Older tutorials often start with `setwd("C:/Users/...")`. That path only exists on one computer, so the script breaks everywhere else. A project folder with `here()` avoids this. - `here()` finds the top of the project by looking for a marker: a `.here` file (the workshop folder has one), an `.Rproj` file, or a `.git` folder. ::: # Part 4: Importing data ## `import()` + `here()` `rio::import()` reads almost any file type (`.csv`, `.xlsx`, `.txt`, SPSS, Stata, SAS, ...). It works out the type from the file extension, so you only need to learn one function. Save the result with `<-`, or it only prints to the Console and is gone. ::: follow-along **👀 Follow along 4.1** — Import `raw_data/linelist_raw.xlsx` and call it `linelist_raw`. Pattern: `NEW_NAME <- import(here("FOLDER", "FILE_NAME.EXTENSION"))` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} linelist_raw <- import(here("raw_data", "linelist_raw.xlsx")) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip icon=false} ## 🧩 Reading a function call Here is the line you just ran, taken apart: `linelist_raw <- import(here("raw_data", "linelist_raw.xlsx"))` | Piece | What it is | What it does | |---|---|---| | `linelist_raw` | the name of a new object | holds the result | | `<-` | the assignment arrow | saves the result in `linelist_raw` | | `import(...)` | a function from the rio package | reads a file into R | | `here(...)` | a function from the here package, used as the **argument** of `import()` | builds the full path to the file | | `"raw_data"`, `"linelist_raw.xlsx"` | two text arguments of `here()` | the folder, then the file name | R runs it from the **inside out**: first `here()` builds the path, then `import()` reads the file at that path, and finally `<-` saves the result. Reading code aloud in the same order helps: "`linelist_raw` gets: import the file at here, raw_data, linelist_raw.xlsx." ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## 🔍 What this code does - `import()` saw the `.xlsx` ending and read the file as an Excel workbook (the first sheet, unless you ask for another). - Nothing prints. `linelist_raw` appears in the **Variables** pane with 6604 rows and 12 columns. - The result is a **data frame**: the same kind of table as `patients` in Part 1, only bigger. Each row is one patient (a case), and each column is one piece of information about them. ::: ::: callout-warning ## Common mistakes - File names must match exactly, including capitals and the extension. - "Error: No such file" means the folder or file name is misspelled, or the workshop folder isn't open (check the **Explorer** on the left). ::: ::: callout-tip ## Other import options you may see - **Base R:** `read.csv()` — older, slower, and needs more settings - **readr:** `read_csv()` — the tidyverse version, fast and returns a tibble - **haven:** `read_sav()`, `read_dta()`, `read_sas()` — SPSS, Stata, SAS files - **Excel files with several sheets:** `import(here("raw_data", "file.xlsx"), which = "Sheet2")` ::: ::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false} ## ✏️ TRY IT 2 (2 min): import the practice data Import the practice data `raw_data/measles_raw.csv` and call it `measles_raw`. ✅ **Check:** in the **Variables** pane, `measles_raw` shows 1215 rows and 11 columns ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false} ## Show solution ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} measles_raw <- import(here("raw_data", "measles_raw.csv")) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## 📖 Good to know - `import()` passes the work to a specialist package based on the file ending: **readxl** for Excel, **data.table** for CSV and text files, and **haven** for SPSS, Stata, and SAS. You only need to remember one function. - `import()` returns a plain **data frame**, which prints every row. That's why this lesson wraps long output in `head()`. Tidyverse functions return a **tibble**, a data frame that prints only the first 10 rows. - Excel stores dates as date-times, so most date columns arrive as ``. One column, `date.onset`, arrives as text: Excel files often hold surprises like this, which is why you inspect before you clean. ::: # Part 5: Inspecting data **Always look before you clean.** Inspecting tells you whether the data imported correctly and what needs fixing. These are the questions to answer, for this dataset and for any dataset you work with later: 1. How many rows and columns are there? Is that what you expected? (`dim()`) 2. Are the column names easy to use? Are the column types right: numbers, dates, text? (`glimpse()`) 3. Which columns have missing values? Are there impossible values? (`skim()`) 4. Are the categories spelled consistently? (`count()`) 5. Are there duplicate rows? (Session 3 shows how to check.) Write down every problem you find. The answers become your problem list in Part 6. ## Size and structure ::: follow-along **👀 Follow along 5.1** — The size and structure of `linelist_raw` with `dim()` and `glimpse()`. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dim(linelist_raw) # rows, columns ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6604 12 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} glimpse(linelist_raw) # every column, its type, and the first few values ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 6,604 Columns: 12 $ `Case ID` "5fe599", "8689b7", "11f8ea", "b8812a", "893f25", "b… $ `infection date` 2014-05-08, NA, NA, 2014-05-04, 2014-05-18, 2014-05… $ date.onset "2014-05-13", "2014-05-13", "2014-05-16", "2014-05-1… $ `hosp date` 2014-05-15, 2014-05-14, 2014-05-18, 2014-05-20, 201… $ `date of outcome` NA, 2014-05-18, 2014-05-30, NA, 2014-05-29, 2014-05… $ OUTCOME NA, "Recover", "Recover", NA, "Recover", "Recover", … $ Gender "m", "f", "m", "f", "m", "f", "f", "f", "m", "f", "m… $ hospital "Other", NA, "St. Mark's Maternity Hospital (SMMH)",… $ age "2", "3", "56", "18", "3", "16", "16", "0", "61", "2… $ age_unit "years", "years", "years", "years", "years", "years"… $ wt_kg 27, 25, 91, 41, 36, 56, 47, 0, 86, 69, 67, 84, 68, 4… $ ht_cm 48, 59, 238, 135, 71, 116, 87, 11, 226, 174, 112, 18… ``` ::: ::: In `glimpse()`, the type is shown in angle brackets: `` text, `` number, `` date, `` date-time. ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## 🔍 What this code does - `dim()` gives the size: rows first, then columns (6604 12). - `glimpse()` turns the table on its side: one line per column, with its name, its type, and the first few values. It's the easiest way to see every column of a wide dataset. - The column names are listed exactly as they're spelled. Code has to use exactly this spelling. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false} ## 🤔 Think about it: what is wrong with these column names? Spaces, dots, capitals, and a mix of styles (`Case ID`, `date.onset`, `OUTCOME`). They are hard to type and need special handling. We fix all of them in Session 2 with one function. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false} ## 🤔 Think about it: which column types look wrong? - `date.onset` is `` (text) but the other dates are `` (date-time) - `age` is `` — it should be a number - There is an `age_unit` column — are all ages in years? ::: ::: callout-tip ## Other ways to look (reading only) You don't need to type these, but you'll see them in other people's code: - `view(linelist_raw)` opens the data like a spreadsheet in the Data Explorer. You can also click the table icon next to `linelist_raw` in the **Variables** pane. Sorting and filtering there doesn't change the data. - `names(linelist_raw)` lists only the column names. - `head(linelist_raw)` shows the first 6 rows; `head(linelist_raw, 10)` shows 10. ::: ## Summary of every column ::: follow-along **👀 Follow along 5.2** — `skim(linelist_raw)`. Look at `n_missing`, and the min and max of `wt_kg` and `ht_cm`. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} skim(linelist_raw) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} Table: Data summary | | | |:------------------------|:------------| |Name |linelist_raw | |Number of rows |6604 | |Number of columns |12 | |_______________________ | | |Column type frequency: | | |character |7 | |numeric |2 | |POSIXct |3 | |________________________ | | |Group variables |None | **Variable type: character** |skim_variable | n_missing| complete_rate| min| max| empty| n_unique| whitespace| |:-------------|---------:|-------------:|---:|---:|-----:|--------:|----------:| |Case ID | 130| 0.98| 6| 6| 0| 5888| 0| |date.onset | 286| 0.96| 10| 10| 0| 580| 0| |OUTCOME | 1493| 0.77| 5| 7| 0| 2| 0| |Gender | 317| 0.95| 1| 1| 0| 2| 0| |hospital | 1509| 0.77| 5| 36| 0| 13| 0| |age | 100| 0.98| 1| 2| 0| 75| 0| |age_unit | 0| 1.00| 5| 6| 0| 2| 0| **Variable type: numeric** |skim_variable | n_missing| complete_rate| mean| sd| p0| p25| p50| p75| p100|hist | |:-------------|---------:|-------------:|------:|-----:|---:|---:|---:|---:|----:|:-----| |wt_kg | 0| 1| 52.69| 18.59| -11| 41| 54| 66| 111|▁▃▇▅▁ | |ht_cm | 0| 1| 125.25| 49.57| 4| 91| 130| 159| 295|▂▅▇▂▁ | **Variable type: POSIXct** |skim_variable | n_missing| complete_rate|min |max |median | n_unique| |:---------------|---------:|-------------:|:----------|:----------|:----------|--------:| |infection date | 2315| 0.65|2012-04-09 |2015-04-27 |2014-10-04 | 538| |hosp date | 0| 1.00|2012-04-20 |2015-04-30 |2014-10-15 | 570| |date of outcome | 1061| 0.84|2012-05-14 |2015-06-04 |2014-10-26 | 575| ::: ::: Look at the `n_missing` column, the minimum of `wt_kg` (below zero!), and the maximum of `ht_cm` (almost 3 meters!). ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## 🔍 What this code does - `skim()` summarizes every column at once, grouped by type: text (`character`), numbers (`numeric`), and date-times (`POSIXct`). - `n_missing` is the number of missing values in each column; `complete_rate` is the share that is filled in. - For numbers, `p0` is the smallest value, `p50` the median, and `p100` the largest. Here the smallest weight is -11 kg and the tallest height is 295 cm: both impossible. - For text, `n_unique` is the number of different values. A high number in a column that should have only a few categories is a sign of misspellings. ::: ::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false} ## ✏️ TRY IT 3 (4 min): size, structure, and summary Use `dim()`, `glimpse()`, and `skim()` on `measles_raw`. a) Which column should be a number but is stored as text (``)? b) Which column names will need backticks? c) In `skim()`, find `Temp (C)`. What is its largest value (`p100`)?
